topics.name: Comparisons with like and as ... as
Relative pronouns who / which / that / whose

options: The train ran as fast like the wind.
The train ran as faster as the wind.
The train ran as fast as the wind.
questions.rule: A comparison of equals uses as + adjective + as: as fast as. Don't mix it with like or use -er.

options: There are two cows in the meadow.
There is two cows in the meadow.
There are two cow in the meadow.
questions.rule: Two cows is plural, so use There are and the plural noun cows.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.

options: who
whom
whose

questions.rule: For a person (a woman) use who as the subject: a woman who was selling flowers. Which is for things.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.

options: is
were
been

questions.rule: A tramp is one person, so use There is: There is a tramp standing near the gate.

options: like
than
as
questions.rule: as ... as always comes in a pair: as cold as ice.

options: is
have
has
questions.rule: Present perfect = has/have + past participle. Meera is one person, so use has: has just boarded.

questions.prompt: Make a sentence in the present perfect.
questions.rule: has + just + past participle tells us something happened a moment ago: has just reached.

chat: What can you see from the train window?
options: I can see a river. There is cows near it.
I can see a river. There are cows near it.
I can sees a river. There are cows near it.
questions.rule: Cows is plural, so There are cows. After can use the base verb: can see.

chat: How fast was the express train?
options: It was as fast than an arrow!
It was as fast as an arrow!
It was more fast as an arrow!
questions.rule: To say two things are equal, use as fast as. Than goes only with a comparative like faster.

questions.source: The bus is slower than the train.
options: The bus is not as faster as the train.
The bus is not as fast as the train.
The bus is not as fast than the train.
questions.rule: slower than = not as fast as. Keep the plain adjective between the two as words.

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence with the correct relative pronoun.
options: I saw a mill who stood by the river.
I saw a mill which stood by the river.
I saw a mill whom stood by the river.
questions.rule: A mill is a thing, so use which (or that): a mill which stood by the river.

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence with the correct tense.
options: We have already cross three bridges.
We has already crossed three bridges.
We have already crossed three bridges.
questions.rule: Present perfect = have/has + past participle. With We use have crossed.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.

options: as
like
then

questions.rule: as ... as is a pair: as slow as a snail. Than is used only after a comparative like slower.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.

options: saw
sees
seen

questions.rule: After has we need the past participle: has never seen, not the base form see.

options: who
whose
which
questions.rule: A cart is a thing, so use which: the cart which ran away.

options: are
is
am
questions.rule: The real subject comes after Here: the daisies is plural, so Here are the daisies.
who comes right after the person it describes: the farmer who was milking cows.

chat: Have you packed your bag for the trip?
options: Yes, I have packed it already.
Yes, I have pack it already.
Yes, I has packed it already.
questions.rule: Answer a Have you ...? question with I have + past participle: I have packed.

questions.source: Here is a child. He is gathering brambles.
options: Here is a child who he is gathering brambles.
Here is a child who is gathering brambles.
Here is a child which is gathering brambles.
questions.rule: who replaces He, so drop the pronoun: a child who is gathering brambles.

questions.prompt: Rewrite using 'not as ... as' without changing the meaning.
questions.source: The aeroplane is faster than the train.
options: The train is not as faster as the aeroplane.
The aeroplane is not as fast as the train.
The train is not as fast as the aeroplane.
questions.rule: Start with the slower one: The train is not as fast as the aeroplane. Swapping the nouns would change the meaning.

options: The meadow was as green as an emerald.
The meadow was green as like an emerald.
The meadow was as greener as an emerald.
questions.rule: Use the plain adjective inside as ... as: as green as an emerald.

options: There was many people at the station yesterday.
There were many people at the station yesterday.
There were many people at the station tomorrow.
questions.rule: Many people is plural and yesterday is past, so use There were.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.

options: am
is
were

questions.rule: The subject is The girl (one person), so the verb is is: The girl whose bag I found is my cousin.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.

options: from
for
during

questions.rule: Use for with a length of time (for five years) and since with a starting point (since 2020).

options: has read
had reading
have read
questions.rule: already goes with the present perfect. With I use have read.
Present perfect question: Have + you + ever + past participle: Have you ever seen ...?
that joins the extra detail to the bridge: the bridge that Grandpa built.

options: He was a Scottish writer who wrote Treasure Island.
He was a Scottish writer which wrote Treasure Island.
He was a Scottish writer who write Treasure Island.
questions.rule: A writer is a person, so use who; the action is past, so who wrote.

chat: Is there a shop near the station?
options: Yes, there are a small tea stall next to it.
Yes, there is a small tea stall next of it.
Yes, there is a small tea stall next to it.
questions.rule: A small tea stall is singular, so there is. The phrase is next to, not next of.

options: Ravi has not finish his homework.
Ravi did not finished his homework.
Ravi has not finished his homework.
questions.rule: Put not after has and keep the past participle: has not finished.

options: This is the best journey I have ever had.
This is the most good journey I have ever had.
This is the best journey I have ever have.
questions.rule: good - better - best is irregular. With ever use the present perfect: I have ever had.

options: The children were as busy as bees.
The children were as busy as a bees.
The children was as busy as bees.
questions.rule: Children is plural, so were. A cannot go with the plural bees: as busy as bees.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.

options: is
were
has

questions.rule: The subject is All the stations (plural), so the verb is were, even after the which clause.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.

options: hasn't
haven't
weren't

questions.rule: The tag uses the same helper as the sentence: You have seen ... takes haven't you?

questions.before: Of all the sights, the river was the
options: more
most
very
questions.rule: Of all compares more than two things, so use the superlative: the most beautiful.

options: have travelled on
has travelled on
travelled on
questions.rule: Last year is a finished past time, so use the simple past travelled, not the present perfect.
Comparing two things: comparative + than: flies higher than birds.

chat: Which is longer, the bridge or the tunnel?
options: The tunnel is longer than the bridge.
The tunnel is more longer than the bridge.
The tunnel is longest than the bridge.
questions.rule: For two things use the comparative longer than. Never add more to an -er word.

questions.source: No other river in India is as long as the Ganga.
options: The Ganga is longest than any other river in India.
The Ganga is longer than any other river in India.
The Ganga is more longer than any other river in India.
questions.rule: Positive No other ... as long as becomes comparative longer than any other.

questions.source: We crossed a bridge. It was very old.
options: We crossed a bridge which it was very old.
We crossed a bridge who was very old.
We crossed a bridge which was very old.
questions.rule: which replaces It, so don't repeat the pronoun: a bridge which was very old.

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence with the correct tense.
options: Grandpa has worked at the station since 1995.
Grandpa has worked at the station for 1995.
Grandpa is working at the station since 1995.
questions.rule: since + a starting point (1995) goes with the present perfect has worked; for needs a length of time.

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence with the correct relative pronoun.
options: That is the boy who's kite got stuck in the tree.
That is the boy whose kite got stuck in the tree.
That is the boy whom kite got stuck in the tree.
questions.rule: whose shows ownership (the boy's kite). who's means who is.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.

options: bridge's
bridges
bridged

questions.rule: one of the + superlative is always followed by a plural noun: one of the longest bridges.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.

options: coming
come
arrives

questions.rule: After here the subject comes after the verb: Rani's two brothers is plural, so here come Rani's two brothers.

questions.after: cart ran away was very upset.
options: who
which
whose
questions.rule: The cart belongs to the man, so use the possessive whose: The man whose cart ran away.
How long + present perfect asks about time up to now: How long have you lived ...?

chat: Have you ever travelled on a toy train?
options: Yes, I have travelled on one in Matheran last May.
Yes, I travel on one in Matheran last May.
Yes, I travelled on one in Matheran last May.
questions.rule: A question with ever uses the present perfect, but a fixed past time (last May) needs the simple past: I travelled.

chat: What was the most exciting part of your trip?
options: The tunnel, which was darker than night, was the most exciting part.
The tunnel, which was more darker than night, was the most exciting part.
The tunnel, who was darker than night, was the most exciting part.
questions.rule: Use darker than (never more darker) and which for a thing like a tunnel.

questions.source: Very few sights are as lovely as a rainbow.
options: A rainbow is one of the loveliest sight.
A rainbow is one of the loveliest sights.
A rainbow is one of the most loveliest sights.
questions.rule: Very few ... as lovely as becomes one of the loveliest + plural noun: one of the loveliest sights.

questions.source: The train has left the station.
options: Has the train left the station?
Has the train leave the station?
Did the train has left the station?
questions.rule: Move has before the subject and keep the past participle: Has the train left ...?
